title: When should a robot correct its own move?
lead: In a simulated kitchen, a Beijing research team tested whether software could spot a pan on the wrong burner and tell the robot to move it. Checking the result helped complete more tasks.

news.title: The object looks the same. The robot may need a different command.
news.summary: Yunbei Zhang and colleagues tested how a robot could respond to a heavier load or a weaker arm in a computer simulation. Their method looks at the movement that already happened and adjusts the next command.
news.details: The RoboAda authors tested command adaptation under changes in load, delay or actuator response in simulation.
news.technical_novelty: The method compares observed movement with the reference robot’s response and adjusts the next group of commands.
news.engineering_impact: The method sits around a trained controller and leaves its weights fixed.
news.limitations: The simulated averages do not measure reliability on physical hardware.
news.evidence_status: The authors reported the experimental protocol and numbers in a preprint.
news.organization: Tulane University, New York University, Nanyang Technological University, MIT and Harvard University
news.body:
Yunbei Zhang and colleagues designed a way for robots to adjust to changes that their cameras cannot show. They simulated changes in the behaviour of a robot or the properties of an object, then checked whether adjusting the commands helped the robot finish. Their correction method is called RoboAda.

After each group of commands, the method collects observations of how the simulated robot actually moved. A model of inverse dynamics estimates which commands the reference robot would have needed to produce that observed movement. The method then compares the estimate with the commands it sent. It uses that evidence to reweight hypotheses about the change in motion, including the possibility that the robot is responding normally. The result is a correction to the next group of commands.

The authors tested five trained controllers in LIBERO, a suite of simulated manipulation tasks, under eleven changes in physical conditions. Their average success rose from 27.8% to 62.9%. In a second simulator, RoboTwin 2.0, they tested two-armed tasks with systematic offsets in the target joint angles. Success there rose from 24.9% to 78.8%. Both results come from experiments with simulated robots.

An empty box can look like a full one, for example, but the difference matters the moment you start lifting. This method gets its clue after trying a movement. The motion it observes can reveal a mismatch between what was asked and what happened even before there is evidence about the object itself. The study does not show how reliable the correction would be with readings from noisy sensors on a physical robot.

news.title: Ten metres from loading to stacking
news.summary: Bigwave Robotics tested a walking humanoid at a South Korean automotive parts factory. It fed parts into a machine, walked to the outfeed and stacked the finished pieces.
news.details: Bigwave Robotics reported an on-site trial of a bipedal robot at a South Korean automotive parts factory. The robot handled engine parts.
news.technical_novelty: It exchanged work signals with the straightening machine’s controller and walked about ten metres to the outfeed.
news.engineering_impact: The trial linked loading, walking and stacking to the cycle of existing equipment.
news.limitations: The announcement gives no cycle count, line rate or performance over a shift.
news.evidence_status: The supplier described the trial, and trade publication Robot News covered the company’s report.
news.body:
Bigwave Robotics assigned a bipedal robot two jobs at an automotive supplier in South Korea. At one station it fed engine parts into a machine. At the other it picked them up after processing. The company tested whether one robot could walk between those places and do both jobs at the appropriate time.

According to Bigwave, the robot picked up engine parts and fed them into a straightening machine, which corrects the shape of a part. Once the machine completed its operation, the robot walked about ten metres to the outfeed and stacked the finished parts on a transfer cart. It exchanged work signals with the machine’s programmable logic controller, an industrial computer that sequences the machine’s operations and coordinates signals with other equipment.

The company connected Hyper Foundry, its robotics software platform, to NVIDIA tools for simulation and training. In millions of simulated runs it trained walking through reinforcement learning, in which actions are selected based on feedback about results. For grasping it used examples of the desired movements, helped by a separate model that locates parts. The company then transferred what it had trained in simulation to the physical robot for the on-site trial.

Walking the distance and turning up at the right time are distinct challenges. A simulation can provide practice at taking steps, but work on a real line depends on knowing where the machine is in its cycle. Signals from its controller supply that information. The company described the exchange and said it would release video. Its report leaves open how many complete sequences the robot performed without an operator stepping in.

news.title: Five minutes to move beans one at a time
news.summary: Organizers in Japan named five judges for a contest in which robotic hands will transfer roasted beans. Each team will use chopsticks or tweezers in a five-minute test.
news.details: Organizers in Japan named five judges for a competition in which robotic hands will transfer roasted beans.
news.technical_novelty: Teams can direct the hand remotely or have a trained program control it.
news.engineering_impact: The shared task and time limit give teams a way to try different approaches to handling small objects.
news.limitations: The final is scheduled for March 26, 2027. The announcement concerns the judges; there are no entrant results yet.
news.evidence_status: The organizers published the judges, eligibility and dates.
news.organization: GMO Internet Group, GMO AIR and Singularity Society
news.body:
GMO Internet Group and its partners announced the judges of a robot hand contest in Tokyo. The timed task sounds simple: move roasted beans one at a time from plate to plate. A robotic hand will have to hold chopsticks or tweezers and use them to pick up each bean accurately.

GMO Internet Group, its robotics company GMO AIR and the Singularity Society announced the judges on November 20. The five include engineer and entrepreneur Satoshi Nakajima and Telexistence co-founder Motoki Sano. Contestants have five minutes to move roasted beans one at a time between plates using chopsticks or tweezers held by a robotic hand with several fingers. Both remote control by a person and control by a program trained in advance are permitted.

The prize pool totals ¥10 million. Applications close on December 18, 2026, and the final is scheduled for March 26, 2027, in Tokyo. The organizers offer participants access to equipment at a laboratory in Shibuya as well as tools for control and training. The rules allow teams to bring their own hand, so they can work on how it is built as well as how it is controlled.

With chopsticks there are two things to keep steady: the tool in the fingers and the bean between its tips. If one stick slips in the hand, the tips can drift apart even though the fingers were told to make the same motion. A person controlling the hand remotely and a program trained before the event approach the same problem differently. The competition rules apply a multiplier of 0.5 to remote-control scores and 1.0 to scores from hands that run without an operator.

news.title: How a robot notices a pan on the wrong burner
news.summary: Researchers at the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence built a system that checks the outcome of a robot’s actions. In a simulated kitchen, it noticed a misplaced pan and directed the arm to move it.
news.details: The Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence proposed a system that sequences robot actions and checks how the work is progressing.
news.technical_novelty: In Innata-0, a model generates movements while separate software checks the observed result and calls a recovery routine when needed.
news.engineering_impact: Adding that layer to the same motion model raised success from 60.2% to 65.4% on simulated kitchen tasks.
news.limitations: The simulated result applies to a specific test suite. Transfer to other robots and settings needs separate testing.
news.evidence_status: The authors documented their comparison and examples of recovery in a preprint.
news.body:
The Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence tested what happens when a robot has to check the outcome as well as move an object. In its simulated kitchen, an arm can grasp a pan successfully and still set it down on the wrong burner. In the system called Innata-0, separate software looks at the resulting scene and can call a recovery routine.

In Innata-0, a world-action model interprets the scene, predicts changes and generates movement commands. It gets the full instruction, the current subtask and a record of confirmed progress. The other component, which the researchers call an agent, organizes the steps and compares the observed scene after a movement with the intended result. When it detects a mismatch, it can invoke a recovery routine and then return to the original task.

In RoboCasa365, a collection of simulated kitchen tasks, the researchers compared two setups using the same movement model. Overall success reached 60.2% without the agent and 65.4% with it. For combinations of steps the model had not seen before, success rose from 32.4% to 43.6%. One example in the paper shows the system noticing a misplaced pan and moving it onto the intended burner.

A pan’s position is something the program can inspect after a movement. In a task spanning several actions, it also has to keep track of the intended burner and which previous steps were finished. That information helps it decide whether to repeat a step or move on. If a camera cannot see the target area, or a needed condition cannot be judged visually, another way to check it would be needed. The study does not measure how often that happens outside its selected tasks.

news.title: Why Amazon wants software for its own AI chips
news.summary: Amazon agreed to buy Decart technology that helps adapt computation to particular chips. The software could affect how developers train and run models used for robotics.
news.details: Amazon signed an agreement to buy Decart’s optimization technology and said it plans to hire the founders and team.
news.technical_novelty: The software helps map model computation to specific chips, including Amazon’s Trainium hardware.
news.engineering_impact: The agreement is relevant to teams choosing computing platforms for training and running robotics models.
news.limitations: Closing requires regulatory clearance. Amazon did not disclose financial terms or comparative benchmarks.
news.evidence_status: Amazon announced the agreement. Reuters independently reported that the company declined to disclose the price.
news.body:
Amazon signed an agreement to acquire Decart technology. It helps programs that do a lot of computation run on different chips. Robotics developers use that kind of processing to learn from recordings of movements, for instance, and then to put the resulting model to work on new images from a camera.

Amazon announced the signed agreement on November 23. It covers the technology behind the Decart Optimization Stack, software that matches the work a model does to the hardware doing the calculation. Amazon also plans to hire Decart’s three co-founders and its researchers and engineers. The teams have worked together since 2025 on Amazon’s Trainium computing chips. Amazon names world models, programs that learn to predict how a scene can change after an action, among the relevant workloads.

Amazon did not disclose the price. Reuters reported that Bloomberg put it at about $7.5 billion, citing a person familiar with the deal. Amazon did not confirm that figure. The deal remains subject to customary closing conditions, including regulatory clearance. Amazon describes reducing cost and increasing speed as goals and did not publish a comparative benchmark for a specific robotics workload.

Think of dividing a big calculation among several workers. Changing the equipment affects how many pieces can be done at once and how long it takes to pass intermediate answers around. In a chip, that work involves computing units and memory, with software deciding how to organize it. Amazon did not give a worked example that shows how much faster a particular robotics model could be trained after the planned acquisition.

technology_signal.title: Checking the result between robot movements
technology_signal.summary: The Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence compared two setups in a simulated kitchen. They used the same movement model, and success rose from 60.2% to 65.4% when verification and recovery were added.
technology_signal.implications: The software compares what it sees with the instruction before moving on. A condition that cannot be judged from a camera image would need another way to be checked.
